Traveling Wave Solutions of Degenerate Coupled KdV EquationThanks: Email:aslipekcan@hacettepe.edu.tr

Metin Gürses ††thanks: gurses@fen.bilkent.edu.tr Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, Faculty of Science Affiliation: Bilkent University, 06800 Ankara - Turkey Affiliation: Aslı Pekcan Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, Faculty of Science Affiliation: Hacettepe University, 06800 Ankara - Turkey
Abstract

We give a detailed study of the traveling wave solutions of (ℓ=2)(\ell=2) Kaup-Boussinesq type of coupled KdV equations. Depending upon the zeros of a fourth degree polynomial, we have cases where there exist no nontrivial real solutions, cases where asymptotically decaying to a constant solitary wave solutions, and cases where there are periodic solutions. All such possible solutions are given explicitly in the form of Jacobi elliptic functions. Graphs of some exact solutions in solitary wave and periodic shapes are exhibited. Extension of our study to the cases ℓ=3\ell=3 and ℓ=4\ell=4 are also mentioned.

Keywords: Traveling wave solution, Degenerate coupled KdV equation, Jacobi elliptic functions

1 Introduction

Multi-component Kaup-Boussinesq (KB) equations can be obtained from the Lax operator

L=D2−∑k=1ℓλk−1​qk​(x,t),L=D^{2}-\sum_{k=1}^{\ell}\lambda^{k-1}q^{k}(x,t), (1.1)

where qk​(x,t)q^{k}(x,t), k=1,2,…,ℓk=1,2,...,\ell are the multi-KB fields [1]-[4]. Here ℓ≥2\ell\geq 2 is a positive integer.

The multi system of KB equation is given as

ut\displaystyle\displaystyle u_{t} =\displaystyle= 32​u​ux+qx2\displaystyle\frac{3}{2}uu_{x}+q_{x}^{2}
qt2\displaystyle q_{t}^{2} =\displaystyle= q2​ux+12​u​qx2+qx3\displaystyle q^{2}u_{x}+\frac{1}{2}uq_{x}^{2}+q_{x}^{3}
⋮⋮⋮\displaystyle\quad\vdots\quad\quad\vdots\quad\quad\vdots
qtℓ−1\displaystyle q_{t}^{\ell-1} =\displaystyle= qℓ−1​ux+12​u​qxℓ−1+vx\displaystyle q^{\ell-1}u_{x}+\frac{1}{2}uq_{x}^{\ell-1}+v_{x}
vt\displaystyle v_{t} =\displaystyle= −14​ux​x​x+v​ux+12​u​vx,\displaystyle-\frac{1}{4}u_{xxx}+vu_{x}+\frac{1}{2}uv_{x}, (1.2)

where q1=uq^{1}=u and qℓ=vq^{\ell}=v. This system in (1.2) was shown to be also a degenerate KdV system of rank one [5]-[7]. This system admits also recursion operator for all values of ℓ\ell. In this work we shall investigate the traveling wave solutions of these coupled equations. For this purpose we start with the case ℓ=2\ell=2. To find such solutions we use time and space translation symmetries of the coupled system.

The KB equation for ℓ=2\ell=2 is

ut\displaystyle u_{t} =\displaystyle= 32​u​ux+vx\displaystyle\frac{3}{2}uu_{x}+v_{x}
vt\displaystyle v_{t} =\displaystyle= −14​ux​x​x+v​ux+12​u​vx.\displaystyle-\frac{1}{4}u_{xxx}+vu_{x}+\frac{1}{2}uv_{x}. (1.3)

In [8] the inverse problem of the above system was studied and soliton solutions which decay asymptotically were found. The N=1N=1 solution found in that work corresponds to the interaction of two solitary waves. It was also mentioned in [8] that there is no solution in the form of traveling wave. Here in this work we prove that there exists no asymptotically vanishing traveling wave solutions of system of equations for ℓ=2\ell=2. This is consistent with the observation of [8]. We show that this is also valid for ℓ=4\ell=4. We claim it to be true for all even positive integers. We show that it is possible to find solitary wave solutions of (1.3) which asymptotically decay to non-zero constants. Furthermore in addition to the solitary wave solutions of (1.3) we find all traveling wave solutions which are expressible in terms of Jacobi elliptic functions.

Traveling wave solutions of a system of equations can be obtained if the equations possess time and space translation symmetries. Such symmetries exist in our case. Hence letting x−c​t=ξx-ct=\xi where cc is a constant (the speed of the wave) and u⁡(x,t)=f⁡(ξ)u(x,t)=f(\xi), and v⁡(x,t)=g⁡(ξ)v(x,t)=g(\xi) from the first equation of (1.3) we have

−c​f′=32​f​f′+g′,\displaystyle-cf^{\prime}=\frac{3}{2}ff^{\prime}+g^{\prime},

which gives

g⁡(ξ)=−c​f−34​f2+d1,\displaystyle g(\xi)=-cf-\frac{3}{4}f^{2}+d_{1}, (1.4)

where d1d_{1} is an integration constant. Using g⁡(ξ)g(\xi) in the second equation of (1.3) yields

−14​f′′′−3​c​f​f′−32​f2​f′+(d1−c2)​f′=0.\displaystyle-\frac{1}{4}f^{\prime\prime\prime}-3cff^{\prime}-\frac{3}{2}f^{2}f^{\prime}+(d_{1}-c^{2})f^{\prime}=0.

Integrating above equation once we obtain

−14​f′′−32​c​f2−12​f3+(d1−c2)​f+d2=0.\displaystyle-\frac{1}{4}f^{\prime\prime}-\frac{3}{2}cf^{2}-\frac{1}{2}f^{3}+(d_{1}-c^{2})f+d_{2}=0.

By using f′f^{\prime} as an integrating factor, we can integrate once more. Finally we get

(f′)2=−f4−4​c​f3+4​(d1−c2)​f2+8​d2​f+8​d3=F⁡(f),(f^{\prime})^{2}=-f^{4}-4cf^{3}+4(d_{1}-c^{2})f^{2}+8d_{2}f+8d_{3}=F(f), (1.5)

where c,d1,d2,d3c,d_{1},d_{2},d_{3} are constants. These constants can be determined from the initial conditions f⁡(0)f(0), f′​(0)f^{\prime}(0), f′′​(0)f^{\prime\prime}(0) and g⁡(0)g(0). If F⁡(f)F(f) has zeros, these zeros are related to these initial conditions. For asymptotically decaying solutions of (ℓ=2)(\ell=2) KB equations ff, f′f^{\prime}, f′′f^{\prime\prime}, f′′′f^{\prime\prime\prime}, gg, and g′g^{\prime} go to zero as ξ→±∞\xi\rightarrow\pm\infty. Here in this work we shall find all possible solutions ff of (1.5). Given a solution ff one can find the corresponding solution g⁡(ξ)g(\xi) from (1.4).

In [9] and [10], a KB like system

ht+(u​h)x+14​ux​x​x=0,\displaystyle h_{t}+(uh)_{x}+\frac{1}{4}\,u_{xxx}=0,
ut+u​ux+hx=0,\displaystyle u_{t}+uu_{x}+h_{x}=0, (1.6)

was considered. Traveling wave solutions of this system satisfy a differential equation like (1.5) but the corresponding polynomial F1​(f)F_{1}(f) is asymptotically positive definite. This means that the above KB like system possesses asymptotically decaying traveling wave solutions. In [9] and [10] some solitary wave solutions were found. The fourth degree polynomial arising in traveling wave solutions of the system (1.6) is different than the one given in (1.5). Hence the behavior of solutions here in this work and in Refs. [9] and [10] are different.

In [11] a modified version of the system (1.6), i.e.

ht+(u​h)x±14​ε2​ux​x​x=0,\displaystyle h_{t}+(uh)_{x}\pm\frac{1}{4}\,\varepsilon^{2}\,u_{xxx}=0,
ut+u​ux+hx=0,\displaystyle u_{t}+uu_{x}+h_{x}=0, (1.7)

was considered, where ε\varepsilon is a parameter which controls the dispersion effects. The upper sign is for the case when the gravity force dominates over the capillary one, and the lower sign is for the opposite case when capillary dominates over the gravity. The traveling wave solutions of the above system (1.7) were considered in [11]. The equation (1.5) becomes now ε2​(f′)2=±F2​(f)\varepsilon^{2}\,(f^{\prime})^{2}=\pm F_{2}(f). In both cases solitary wave solutions (dark and bright solitons) were found in [11]. The lower case (negative sign) resembles to our case. Hence our solution in section 3.13.1 can be considered as a dark soliton in the sense of [11]. This is the solution corresponding one double and two simple zeros of the polynomial F⁡(f)F(f). We have all other solutions corresponding to different combinations of the zeros of F⁡(f)F(f) in sections 33, 44, and 55.

The layout of our paper is as follows: In section 22, we study the behavior of the solutions in the neighborhood of the zeros of F⁡(f)F(f) and discuss all possible cases. We find all solitary wave solutions of the system (1.3) in section 33. These correspond to one double and two simple zeros of F⁡(f)F(f), and one triple and one simple zeros of F⁡(f)F(f). In section 44, we find all elliptic type of solutions starting from very special ones to the most general elliptic type of solutions. These solutions are given in terms of the zeros of the function F⁡(f)F(f). In section 55, we discuss ℓ=3\ell=3 and ℓ=4\ell=4 cases. In section 66, we give the graphs of the solutions corresponding to all cases considered in the text.

2 General waves of permanent form for (ℓ=2)(\ell=2)

Proposition 2.1

There is no real asymptotically vanishing traveling wave solution of the equation (1.3) in the form u⁡(x,t)=f⁡(ξ)u(x,t)=f(\xi) and v⁡(x,t)=g⁡(ξ)v(x,t)=g(\xi), where ξ=x−c​t\xi=x-ct.

Proof. If we apply the boundary conditions f,f′,f′′,f′′′,g,g′→0f,f^{\prime},f^{\prime\prime},f^{\prime\prime\prime},g,g^{\prime}\rightarrow 0 as ξ→±∞\xi\rightarrow\pm\infty which describe the solitary wave, we get d1=d2=d3=0d_{1}=d_{2}=d_{3}=0. Hence we end up with

(f′)2=−f4−4​c​f3−4​c2​f2\displaystyle(f^{\prime})^{2}=-f^{4}-4cf^{3}-4c^{2}f^{2} =\displaystyle= −f2​(f2+4​c​f+4​c2)\displaystyle-f^{2}(f^{2}+4cf+4c^{2})
=\displaystyle= −f2​(f+2​c)2.\displaystyle-f^{2}(f+2c)^{2}.

Clearly, we do not have a real solution ff. □\Box

Now we will deal with the equation (1.5). In order to have real solutions, d1,d2,d3d_{1},d_{2},d_{3} must take values so that the following inequality holds:

4​d1​f2+8​d2​f+8​d3≥f2​(f+2​c)2.4d_{1}f^{2}+8d_{2}f+8d_{3}\geq f^{2}(f+2c)^{2}.

2.1 Zeros of F⁡(f)F(f) and Types of Solutions

Here we will analyze the zeros of F⁡(f)F(f).

(i)   If f1=f⁡(ξ1)f_{1}=f(\xi_{1}) is a simple zero of F⁡(f)F(f) we have F⁡(f1)=0F(f_{1})=0. Taylor expansion of F⁡(f)F(f) gives

(f′)2=F⁡(f)\displaystyle(f^{\prime})^{2}=F(f) =\displaystyle= F⁡(f1)+F′​(f1)​(f−f1)+O⁡((f−f1)2)\displaystyle F(f_{1})+F^{\prime}(f_{1})(f-f_{1})+O((f-f_{1})^{2})
=\displaystyle= F′​(f1)​(f−f1)+O⁡((f−f1)2).\displaystyle F^{\prime}(f_{1})(f-f_{1})+O((f-f_{1})^{2}).

From here we get f′​(ξ1)=0f^{\prime}(\xi_{1})=0 and f′′​(ξ1)=F′​(f1)/2\displaystyle f^{\prime\prime}(\xi_{1})=F^{\prime}(f_{1})/2. Hence we can write the function f⁡(ξ)f(\xi) as

f⁡(ξ)\displaystyle\displaystyle f(\xi) =\displaystyle= f⁡(ξ1)+(ξ−ξ1)​f′​(ξ1)+12​(ξ−ξ1)2​f′′​(ξ1)+O⁡((ξ−ξ1)3)\displaystyle f(\xi_{1})+(\xi-\xi_{1})f^{\prime}(\xi_{1})+\frac{1}{2}(\xi-\xi_{1})^{2}f^{\prime\prime}(\xi_{1})+O((\xi-\xi_{1})^{3}) (2.1)
=\displaystyle= f1+14​(ξ−ξ1)2​F′​(f1)+O⁡((ξ−ξ1)3).\displaystyle f_{1}+\frac{1}{4}(\xi-\xi_{1})^{2}F^{\prime}(f_{1})+O((\xi-\xi_{1})^{3}).

Thus, in the neighborhood of ξ=ξ1\xi=\xi_{1}, the function f⁡(ξ)f(\xi) has local minimum or maximum as F′​(f1)F^{\prime}(f_{1}) is positive or negative respectively since f′′​(ξ1)=F′​(f1)/2\displaystyle f^{\prime\prime}(\xi_{1})=F^{\prime}(f_{1})/2.

(ii)   If f1=f⁡(ξ1)f_{1}=f(\xi_{1}) is a double zero of F⁡(f)F(f) we have F⁡(f1)=F′​(f1)=0F(f_{1})=F^{\prime}(f_{1})=0. Taylor expansion of F⁡(f)F(f) gives

(f′)2=F⁡(f)\displaystyle\displaystyle(f^{\prime})^{2}=F(f) =\displaystyle= F⁡(f1)+F′​(f1)​(f−f1)+12​(f−f1)2​F′′​(f1)+O⁡((f−f1)3)\displaystyle F(f_{1})+F^{\prime}(f_{1})(f-f_{1})+\frac{1}{2}(f-f_{1})^{2}F^{\prime\prime}(f_{1})+O((f-f_{1})^{3}) (2.2)
=\displaystyle= 12​(f−f1)2​F′′​(f1)+O⁡((f−f1)3).\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}(f-f_{1})^{2}F^{\prime\prime}(f_{1})+O((f-f_{1})^{3}).

To have real solution ff, we should have F′′​(f1)>0F^{\prime\prime}(f_{1})>0. From the equality (2.2) we get

f′±12​f​F′′​(f1)∼±12​f1​F′′​(f1),\displaystyle f^{\prime}\pm\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}f\sqrt{F^{\prime\prime}(f_{1})}\sim\pm\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}f_{1}\sqrt{F^{\prime\prime}(f_{1})},

which gives

f⁡(ξ)∼f1+α​e±12​F′′​(f1)​ξ,\displaystyle f(\xi)\sim f_{1}+\alpha e^{\pm\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\sqrt{F^{\prime\prime}(f_{1})}\xi}, (2.3)

where α\alpha is a constant. Hence f→f1f\rightarrow f_{1} as ξ→∓∞\xi\rightarrow\mp\infty. The solution ff can have only one peak and the wave extends from −∞-\infty to ∞\infty.

(iii)   If f1=f⁡(ξ1)f_{1}=f(\xi_{1}) is a triple zero of F⁡(f)F(f) we have F⁡(f1)=F′​(f1)=F′′​(f1)=0F(f_{1})=F^{\prime}(f_{1})=F^{\prime\prime}(f_{1})=0. Taylor expansion of F⁡(f)F(f) gives

(f′)2\displaystyle\displaystyle(f^{\prime})^{2} =\displaystyle= F⁡(f)\displaystyle F(f) (2.4)
=\displaystyle= F⁡(f1)+F′​(f1)​(f−f1)+12​(f−f1)2​F′′​(f1)+16​(f−f1)3+O⁡((f−f1)4)\displaystyle F(f_{1})+F^{\prime}(f_{1})(f-f_{1})+\frac{1}{2}(f-f_{1})^{2}F^{\prime\prime}(f_{1})+\frac{1}{6}(f-f_{1})^{3}+O((f-f_{1})^{4})
=\displaystyle= 16​(f−f1)3​F′′′​(f1)+O⁡((f−f1)4).\displaystyle\frac{1}{6}(f-f_{1})^{3}F^{\prime\prime\prime}(f_{1})+O((f-f_{1})^{4}).

This is valid only if both signs of (f−f1)3(f-f_{1})^{3} and F′′′​(f1)F^{\prime\prime\prime}(f_{1}) are same i.e. we have the following two possibilities to have real solution ff:

OPEN1)1) (f−f1)>0(f-f_{1})>0 and F′′′​(f1)>0,F^{\prime\prime\prime}(f_{1})>0,

OPEN2)2) (f−f1)<0(f-f_{1})<0 and F′′′​(f1)<0.F^{\prime\prime\prime}(f_{1})<0.

Let us analyze these cases. If (f−f1)>0(f-f_{1})>0 and F′′′​(f1)>0F^{\prime\prime\prime}(f_{1})>0 then we have

f′∼±16​(f−f1)3/2​F′′′​(f1),\displaystyle f^{\prime}\sim\pm\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(f-f_{1})^{3/2}\sqrt{F^{\prime\prime\prime}(f_{1})},

which gives

f⁡(ξ)∼f1+4(±16​F′′′​(f1)​ξ+α1)2,\displaystyle f(\xi)\sim f_{1}+\frac{4}{\Big(\pm\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\sqrt{F^{\prime\prime\prime}(f_{1})}\xi+\alpha_{1}\Big)^{2}}, (2.5)

where α1\alpha_{1} is a constant. Thus f→f1f\rightarrow f_{1} as ξ→±∞\xi\rightarrow\pm\infty if F′′′​(f1)>0F^{\prime\prime\prime}(f_{1})>0.

Let (f−f1)<0(f-f_{1})<0 and F′′′​(f1)<0F^{\prime\prime\prime}(f_{1})<0 hold. In this case, (f1−f)>0(f_{1}-f)>0 and F′′′​(f1)=−G⁡(f1)F^{\prime\prime\prime}(f_{1})=-G(f_{1}), G⁡(f1)>0G(f_{1})>0. Then

f′∼±16​(f1−f)3/2​G⁡(f1),\displaystyle f^{\prime}\sim\pm\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(f_{1}-f)^{3/2}\sqrt{G(f_{1})},

which yields

f⁡(ξ)∼f1−4(±16​G⁡(f1)​ξ+α2)2,\displaystyle f(\xi)\sim f_{1}-\frac{4}{\Big(\pm\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\sqrt{G(f_{1})}\xi+\alpha_{2}\Big)^{2}}, (2.6)

where α2\alpha_{2} is a constant. Thus f→f1f\rightarrow f_{1} as ξ→±∞\xi\rightarrow\pm\infty if F′′′​(f1)=−G⁡(f1)<0F^{\prime\prime\prime}(f_{1})=-G(f_{1})<0.

(iv)  If f1=f⁡(ξ1)f_{1}=f(\xi_{1}) is a quadruple zero of F⁡(f)F(f) then there is only one possibility F⁡(f)=−(f−f1)4=(f′)2F(f)=-(f-f_{1})^{4}=(f^{\prime})^{2}. It is clear that this case does not give a real solution except when f=f1f=f_{1}.

2.2 All Possible Cases

Here we present the sketches of the graphs of F⁡(f)F(f). Real solutions (f′)2=F⁡(f)≥0(f^{\prime})^{2}=F(f)\geq 0 occur in the shaded regions.

Now we analyze all possible cases about the zeros of F⁡(f)F(f) and above graphs.

(1)  No real zero. If there is no real zeros of F⁡(f)F(f) then F⁡(f)<0F(f)<0. Hence there is no real solution of (1.5) in that case.

(2)  Two simple real zeros. If there is a simple zero f1f_{1} of F⁡(f)F(f), since the order of F⁡(f)F(f) is four, there should be another simple zero f2f_{2} of F⁡(f)F(f). The corresponding graph to this case is given in (a)(a). Here, the real solution occurs when ff is between two different simple zeros f1f_{1} and f2f_{2}. At f1f_{1}, F′​(f1)=f′′​(ξ1)>0F^{\prime}(f_{1})=f^{\prime\prime}(\xi_{1})>0 so graph of the function ff is concave up at ξ1\xi_{1}. At f2f_{2}, F′​(f2)=f′′​(ξ2)>0F^{\prime}(f_{2})=f^{\prime\prime}(\xi_{2})>0 hence graph of the function ff is concave up at ξ2\xi_{2}. Thus it is clear that the solution is periodic.

(3)  One double zero. If there is only one double zero f1f_{1} then

(f′)2=−(f−f1)2​(f2+p​f+q),(f^{\prime})^{2}=-(f-f_{1})^{2}(f^{2}+pf+q), (2.7)

where f2+p​f+qf^{2}+pf+q has no real zero. This means p2−4​q<0p^{2}-4q<0 which yields that f2+p​f+q>0f^{2}+pf+q>0. Then (f′)2=−(f−f1)2​(f2+p​f+q)<0(f^{\prime})^{2}=-(f-f_{1})^{2}(f^{2}+pf+q)<0 hence there is no real solution in that case except when f=f1f=f_{1}. Similarly, in the case when F⁡(f)F(f) has two double zeros f1f_{1} and f2f_{2}, no real solutions exist since (f′)2=−(f−f1)2​(f−f2)2<0(f^{\prime})^{2}=-(f-f_{1})^{2}(f-f_{2})^{2}<0 except when f=f1f=f_{1} or f=f2f=f_{2}.

(4)  One double and two simple zeros. The corresponding graphs for this case are (b)(b), (c)(c) and (d)(d). In (b)(b) and (c)(c), there are two different simple zeros f1f_{1} and f3f_{3} and one double zero f2f_{2}. We have f2<f1<f3f_{2}<f_{1}<f_{3} in (b)(b) and in the graph (c)(c), f1<f3<f2f_{1}<f_{3}<f_{2}. In both cases, the real solution occurs when ff is between two simple zeros f1f_{1} and f3f_{3}. At f1f_{1}, F′​(f1)=f′′​(ξ1)>0F^{\prime}(f_{1})=f^{\prime\prime}(\xi_{1})>0 so graph of the function ff is concave up at ξ1\xi_{1}. At f3f_{3}, F′​(f3)=f′′​(ξ3)>0F^{\prime}(f_{3})=f^{\prime\prime}(\xi_{3})>0 hence graph of the function ff is concave up at ξ3\xi_{3}. It is clear that the solution is periodic in this case.

In (d)(d), different than the graphs (b)(b) and (c)(c) we have f1<f2<f3f_{1}<f_{2}<f_{3}. The real solution occurs when ff stays between f1f_{1} and f2f_{2} or f2f_{2} and f3f_{3}. At f1f_{1}, F′​(f1)=f′′​(ξ1)>0F^{\prime}(f_{1})=f^{\prime\prime}(\xi_{1})>0 hence graph of the function ff is concave up at ξ1\xi_{1}. At double zero f2f_{2}, f→f2f\rightarrow f_{2} as ξ→±∞\xi\rightarrow\pm\infty. Hence we have a solitary wave solution with amplitude f1−f2<0f_{1}-f_{2}<0.

Similarly at f3f_{3}, F′​(f3)=f′′​(ξ3)<0F^{\prime}(f_{3})=f^{\prime\prime}(\xi_{3})<0, hence graph of the function ff is concave down at ξ3\xi_{3}. Therefore, we also have a solitary wave solution with amplitude f3−f2>0f_{3}-f_{2}>0. Explicit solitary wave solution for this case can be found in the next section.

(5)   One triple and one simple zero. For this case, we can analyze the graphs (e)(e) and (f)(f). In (e)(e), f1f_{1} is simple and f2f_{2} is triple zeros of F⁡(f)F(f). We see that F′​(f1)=f′′​(ξ1)>0F^{\prime}(f_{1})=f^{\prime\prime}(\xi_{1})>0 hence graph of the function ff is concave up at ξ1\xi_{1}. From the case (iii), we know that f→f2f\rightarrow f_{2} as ξ→±∞\xi\rightarrow\pm\infty for f−f2<0f-f_{2}<0 and F′′′​(f2)<0F^{\prime\prime\prime}(f_{2})<0. Hence we have solitary wave solution with amplitude f1−f2<0f_{1}-f_{2}<0.

Similarly, in (f)(f) we have one triple zero f1f_{1} and one simple zero f2f_{2}. For triple zero f1f_{1} we have f→f1f\rightarrow f_{1} as ξ→±∞\xi\rightarrow\pm\infty for f−f1>0f-f_{1}>0 and F′′′​(f2)>0F^{\prime\prime\prime}(f_{2})>0. For simple zero we have F′​(f2)=f′′​(ξ2)<0F^{\prime}(f_{2})=f^{\prime\prime}(\xi_{2})<0 therefore graph of the function ff is concave down at ξ2\xi_{2}. Clearly, we have a solitary wave solution with amplitude f2−f1>0f_{2}-f_{1}>0. Explicit solitary wave solution for this case can be found in the next section.

(6)  Four different simple zeros. The corresponding graph for this case is given in (g)(g). Here, there are four simple zeros f1<f2<f3<f4f_{1}<f_{2}<f_{3}<f_{4}. For f1f_{1} and f3f_{3}, we have F′​(f1)=f′′​(ξ1)>0F^{\prime}(f_{1})=f^{\prime\prime}(\xi_{1})>0 and F′​(f3)=f′′​(ξ3)>0F^{\prime}(f_{3})=f^{\prime\prime}(\xi_{3})>0 thus graph of the function ff is concave up at ξ1\xi_{1} and ξ3\xi_{3}. For f2f_{2} and f4f_{4}, we have F′​(f2)=f′′​(ξ2)<0F^{\prime}(f_{2})=f^{\prime\prime}(\xi_{2})<0 and F′​(f4)=f′′​(ξ4)<0F^{\prime}(f_{4})=f^{\prime\prime}(\xi_{4})<0 so graph of the function ff is concave down at ξ2\xi_{2} and ξ4\xi_{4}. Obviously, the solution is periodic.

As a summary we have the following results. By solution below, we mean non-constant solutions.

Proposition 2.2

Equation (1.5) has no real solutions when the function F(f) has one of the following properties: (i) it has no real zeros, (ii) it has only two real zeros, (iii) it has only one double zero, (iv) it has only two double zeros, and (v) it has a quadruple zero.

Proposition 2.3

Equation (1.5) admits solitary wave solutions when the function F(f) admits (i) one double and two simple zeros and (ii) one triple and one simple zeros.

From the proposition 2.2 we can conclude that the function F⁡(f)F(f) must have four zeros,

F⁡(f)=−(f−f1)​(f−f2)​(f−f3)​(f−f4).F(f)=-(f-f_{1})(f-f_{2})(f-f_{3})(f-f_{4}).

The constants c,d1,d2,d3c,d_{1},d_{2},d_{3} can be expressed in terms of the zeros of F⁡(f)F(f):

c\displaystyle\displaystyle c =\displaystyle= −f1+f2+f3+f44\displaystyle-\frac{f_{1}+f_{2}+f_{3}+f_{4}}{4}
d1\displaystyle d_{1} =\displaystyle= (f1+f2+f3+f4)216−f1​f2+f2​f4+f2​f3+f1​f4+f1​f3+f3​f44\displaystyle\frac{(f_{1}+f_{2}+f_{3}+f_{4})^{2}}{16}-\frac{f_{1}f_{2}+f_{2}f_{4}+f_{2}f_{3}+f_{1}f_{4}+f_{1}f_{3}+f_{3}f_{4}}{4}
d2\displaystyle d_{2} =\displaystyle= f1​f2​f4+f1​f2​f3+f2​f3​f4+f1​f3​f48\displaystyle\frac{f_{1}f_{2}f_{4}+f_{1}f_{2}f_{3}+f_{2}f_{3}f_{4}+f_{1}f_{3}f_{4}}{8}
d3\displaystyle d_{3} =\displaystyle= −f1​f2​f3​f48.\displaystyle-\frac{f_{1}f_{2}f_{3}f_{4}}{8}. (2.8)

In the next section we shall find the solitary wave solutions mentioned in the above proposition which correspond to special cases of the zeros f1,f2,f3,f4f_{1},f_{2},f_{3},f_{4}.

3 Exact Solitary Wave Solutions

3.1 One double zero and two simple zeros

Let f1f_{1} and f3f_{3} be two different simple zeros and f2f_{2} be a double zero of F⁡(f)F(f). Thus we have

(f′)2=F⁡(f)=−(f−f2)2​(f−f1)​(f−f3).(f^{\prime})^{2}=F(f)=-(f-f_{2})^{2}(f-f_{1})(f-f_{3}).

Let f−f2=uf-f_{2}=u and so f−f1=u−u1f-f_{1}=u-u_{1}, where u1=f1−f2u_{1}=f_{1}-f_{2} and f−f2=u−u3f-f_{2}=u-u_{3}, where u3=f3−f2u_{3}=f_{3}-f_{2}. Hence the above equation becomes

(u′)2=−u2​(u−u1)​(u−u3).(u^{\prime})^{2}=-u^{2}(u-u_{1})(u-u_{3}).

Using the substitution u=1/y\displaystyle u=1/y

=\displaystyle= −u1​u3​(1u1−y)​(1u3−y).\displaystyle-u_{1}u_{3}\Big(\frac{1}{u_{1}}-y\Big)\Big(\frac{1}{u_{3}}-y\Big).

After some arrangements we have

(y′)2=−u1​u3​{[y−12​(1u1+1u3)]2−14​(1u1−1u3)2}.\displaystyle(y^{\prime})^{2}=-u_{1}u_{3}\Big\{\Big[y-\frac{1}{2}\Big(\frac{1}{u_{1}}+\frac{1}{u_{3}}\Big)\Big]^{2}-\frac{1}{4}\Big(\frac{1}{u_{1}}-\frac{1}{u_{3}}\Big)^{2}\Big\}. (3.1)

Using the trigonometric substitution

y−12​(1u1+1u3)=12​(1u1−1u3)​cosh⁡θ\displaystyle y-\frac{1}{2}\Big(\frac{1}{u_{1}}+\frac{1}{u_{3}}\Big)=\frac{1}{2}\Big(\frac{1}{u_{1}}-\frac{1}{u_{3}}\Big)\cosh{\theta}

the equation (3.1) becomes

(θ′)2=−u1​u3.(\theta^{\prime})^{2}=-u_{1}u_{3}.

Conjecture: For all even ℓ\ell, since we have the following equality

the degenerate coupled KdV equation (1.2) does not have real traveling wave solution with asymptotically vanishing boundary conditions.

7 Conclusion

We have studied symmetry reduced (traveling waves) equations of the Kaup-Boussinesq (KB) type of coupled degenerate KdV equations for ℓ=2\ell=2. The reduced equation turns out to be such that the square of the derivative of the dependent variable is equal to a fourth degree polynomial of the dependent variable. There are four arbitrary constants in the polynomial function. We have investigated all possible cases and gave all solitary wave solutions which rapidly decay to some constants of the (ℓ=2)(\ell=2) KB equations. There are periodic solutions of this set of coupled KdV equations in terms of the Jacobi elliptic functions. We first introduced special solutions of this type where the zeros of F⁡(f)F(f) satisfy certain constraints. If we remove these constraints among the zeros we obtained the most general solution in terms of the elliptic functions of KB system under the assumed symmetry. There are four different such solutions which differ by the initial values at the origin. For illustration we have given the graphs of some interesting solutions. We have also initiated the work on the cases for ℓ=3\ell=3 and ℓ=4\ell=4. We have given some results concerning these cases. A detailed study of the traveling wave solutions of the cases ℓ=3\ell=3 and ℓ=4\ell=4 will be communicated later.
